statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for a problem at a later interview, many of them without treatment, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the two samples combined without weighting). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year, many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, whether any had treatment is not reported, and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains it (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% no longer met the full criteria (editors' calculation from unweighted counts), with persistence of 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52; no longer meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). In 21 cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, 15 of them recruited through treatment, followed for 3 to 50 years (mean 17), published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US, 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end were in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; single cohorts ranged from about 20% to 96%, remission was higher in cohorts followed longer, and the 6 cohorts not in treatment at the start did not differ detectably from the treatment cohorts (62% against 51%, p 0.42). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figure mixes very different follow-up times and so describes no particular time point, and the review did not appraise its cohorts (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 published estimates of recovery without treatment (27 studies, 1976–2018, 24 of them North American) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people initially without treatment, 36.0% fell to 14.0% when recovery also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most estimates covered about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, treatment was not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment? Many do, but the numbers depend on how studies count. Of US soldiers in Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they had been dependent on narcotics there; in the year after coming home, about 1 in 100 had been. Whether they had treatment was not recorded. In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later, though some still had a few. In 21 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, on average 17 years later. For alcohol, studies of recovery without treatment give anything from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because they count different groups: among people who have recovered, many were never treated; among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover without treatment in a given year. Most of this is about alcohol or heroin.
population: US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, 15 recruited through treatment, published 2000–2015 (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)

comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples, unweighted, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% not (editors' calculation, unweighted); persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years: standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), cohorts 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (p 0.421); longer follow-up, higher standard rate (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004). Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates: 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission once vs also at 16 years; a US cohort).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a richer, shared living space makes animals take less of a drug, and these animal studies cannot show anything about people. In three small experiments from one laboratory (Simon Fraser University; 1978, 1979 and 1981; the original papers are not read here and are described by a critical history), rats housed together in a large enclosure with sawdust, boxes and tubes ('Rat Park') drank less morphine solution than rats housed alone in small cages, but only under particular conditions: on choice days after a period of forced morphine drinking (1978), with sweetened, weak solutions (1979), and according to the housing at the time of testing, not in early life (1981). During 57 days when morphine solution was their only fluid, the Rat Park rats drank more on average (18.6 against 13.3 mg of morphine hydrochloride per rat, as tabulated), and they did drink morphine, contrary to popular accounts. The groups held 8 to 22 rats, males and females lived together in Rat Park with no account of pregnancies, intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions, and the many comparisons raised the risk of chance findings; the original authors drew cautious conclusions and did not link the results to drug problems in people (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study, each with 10 male and 10 female rats in each housing condition, did not find lower intake in colony rats: in the first, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and no differently at the three weaker ones; in the second, with the colony's intake known only as a group total and no statistical test, isolated rats drank more at three of four strengths, by smaller margins than the up to sevenfold difference described for 1981 (Petrie, 1996). The author's explanation, a change in the supplier's breeding stock, was not tested, and this study too measured intake differently in the two housing conditions. Other housing studies, summarized second-hand, point both ways: in one, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution; in another, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In a different kind of experiment, male rats offered a choice between an intravenous cocaine infusion and a sweet drink almost all came to prefer the sweet drink, also after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine, though they still chose cocaine on about 16% of choices (Lenoir et al., 2007); earlier studies in monkeys, as those authors note, found most monkeys preferring high doses of cocaine to food. Every finding here comes from animals under laboratory conditions; how housing, poverty, opportunity or social exclusion shape drug use and drug problems in people is not shown by these designs. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and drugs? Less than is often said, and only in rats. In the Rat Park studies of 1978 to 1981, rats living together in a big space with things to do drank less morphine water than rats kept alone, but only in some conditions; when morphine water was all they had to drink, the Rat Park rats drank more. The groups were small, and drinking was measured in different ways for the two groups. Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 study did not find less drinking in rats living together. In a different kind of study, rats almost always chose a sweet drink over cocaine. None of this tested people, so it cannot say how where people live shapes their drug use. See the contested question.
population: Laboratory rats: Wistar rats in the three Rat Park experiments of 1978–1981 (groups of 8 to 22; as described by Gage & Sumnall, 2019); 80 outbred Wistar rats of both sexes in two repeat experiments (Petrie, 1996); male Wistar rats in cocaine-choice experiments (Lenoir et al., 2007); no people
exposure: Housing together in a large enclosure or colony box from weaning or at testing ('Rat Park'); in the choice experiments, a sweet drink (saccharin or sucrose water) available as an alternative to cocaine
comparator: Rats housed alone in small standard cages; in the choice experiments, rats offered only the cocaine lever, or water instead of the sweet drink
outcome: Voluntary intake of oral morphine solution (sweetened or not) beside water; choice of intravenous cocaine infusions against the alternative
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of environment. Rat Park, as tabulated by Gage & Sumnall (2019): 1978, forced access (57 days) Rat Park 18.6 vs isolated 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat; Nichols cycles F = 200.9 (df 1/69) and abstinence period F 26.38 (df 1/23), isolated rats drinking more on choice days; 1979, housing difference only with 10% sucrose, largest at 0.15 mg/ml; 1981, housing at testing F = 33.64, p < 0.0001 (df not printed). Petrie (1996), isolated vs colony, grams of morphine solution a day: Experiment 1, 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6 (colony more; F(1, 34) = 80.98 for grams), 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3, 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3, 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8 (no housing difference at these three); Experiment 2 (no test), 0.3 vs 4.3, 9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9, 44.4 vs 33.1; the 1981 difference described as up to sevenfold. Lenoir et al. (2007), male rats, intravenous cocaine (0.25 mg per infusion, study condition) vs 20 s of 0.2% saccharin: saccharin preferred from day 2 (N = 43); rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (drug-naive), 8.3% (first trained on cocaine), none of 11 (after intake escalated from 7.34 to 26.04 mg/day); cocaine chosen on about 15.6% of choices on average.

indirectness.note: Preclinical evidence is always indirect: oral morphine drinking beside water, or a few intravenous cocaine infusions a day in a choice procedure, in one rat strain; cage against colony box is a narrow stand-in for an environment. grade.reasoning: Animal experiments without described random allocation start low (the original Rat Park papers are seen only through a critical history, which adds to the risk of bias because they cannot be appraised). Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. The relation is insufficient evidence: a housing effect on drug intake in rats is neither shown nor excluded. Status contested: the original findings and the direct repeat point in opposite directions, and a credible published critique changes how the originals should be read (METHODS 6.4), so the six-part box applies. The choice experiments of Lenoir et al. (2007) answer a different question (a sweet drink against cocaine) and are kept apart from the housing evidence; their preference is consistent within one procedure, one strain and one sex, and earlier monkey studies point the other way. The critical history misattributes Petrie's repeat to the 1979 study (card reporting issue); the statement names the 1981 study, as Petrie does. Petrie (1996) gives no dates for its experiments, so the repeat is dated by its publication.

debate.question: Does a richer, shared living space make rats take less morphine or cocaine, as the 'Rat Park' story says, and what can such studies say about people?
debate.evidence_yes: In the three Rat Park experiments, as summarized by a critical history, isolated rats drank more morphine solution than colony rats on choice days in the later periods of the 1978 study (Nichols cycles, F = 200.9, df 1/69; abstinence period, F 26.38, df 1/23; both p < 0.001), with sweetened weak solutions in morphine-naive rats in 1979 (largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose), and in 1981 according to the housing at the time of testing, whatever the early housing (F = 33.64, p < 0.0001) (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In the second experiment of the repeat, isolated rats drank more of three of the four morphine solutions (for example 44.4 against 33.1 g a day at the weakest), the direction of the original finding, though without a test (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In choice experiments, almost every male rat came to prefer a sweet drink to intravenous cocaine, across the cocaine doses, delays and costs tested, after escalating intake and during intoxication (2.3% of drug-naive rats, 8.3% of rats first trained on cocaine and none of 11 rats with escalated intake preferred cocaine) (Lenoir et al., 2007). The critical history still calls the core message, that drug problems are more than a biological response to a drug, important (Gage & Sumnall, 2019).
debate.evidence_no: In the 1978 experiment, Rat Park rats drank more morphine than isolated rats during the 57 days when it was their only fluid (18.6 against 13.3 mg per rat, as tabulated), and isolated rats drank less on non-choice days; in 1979 there was little evidence of a housing difference at high morphine and low sugar concentrations; differences appeared only in specific conditions and stages; intake was measured with different methods in the two housing conditions, groups were very small, males and females shared the colony, and many comparisons were made (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). The two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study did not find lower intake in colony rats: in the first, with a statistical test, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and no differently at the weaker ones, and no difference in either experiment came near the up to sevenfold difference described for 1981 (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake, and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In earlier choice studies, most monkeys preferred high doses of cocaine to food, in one study to a sucrose pellet, as Lenoir et al. (2007) note, and the rats' preference for a sweet drink was shown in one strain, one sex and one procedure with eight choices a day.
debate.neither_can_show: None of these studies measured anything in people: a cage against a colony box is a narrow stand-in for a human environment, oral morphine drinking or a few cocaine infusions a day is not human drug use, and housing, poverty, opportunity, social exclusion and access to services, which matter for people, were not studied. Even for rats, measuring intake by different methods in the two housing conditions (in the originals and in the repeat) means that part of any difference could come from the measuring; the explanation offered for the failed repeat (a change in the rats' breeding stock) was not tested; and no study read here allocated rats to housing at random and measured intake the same way in both groups.
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading: the popular account, that rats in a rich environment refuse morphine, is not what the original papers reported, since Rat Park rats did drink morphine and drank more of it when it was their only fluid. The housing effect rests on three small experiments from one laboratory with a built-in measurement difference, and the one direct repeat did not reproduce it, so whether housing changes drug taking in rats is not settled; certainty very low. That a sweet drink can win over cocaine in a choice procedure is a separate rat finding, consistent within one procedure but contradicted by earlier monkey studies. For people, these studies can only suggest questions; the evidence in people is of other kinds (see the answers on recovery from drug and alcohol problems and on whether people choose other rewards over cocaine).
debate.what_would_settle_it: For rats: a preregistered, adequately powered replication with random allocation to colony or isolated housing, the same automated individual measurement of intake in both conditions, both sexes housed so that litters cannot occur, blinded analysis and more than one strain or supplier. For people: longitudinal or natural-experiment studies of how housing, opportunity and social exclusion change the course of drug use.

statement: In six people who smoked cocaine almost daily, living on an inpatient research unit, cocaine was chosen over a $5 voucher on most occasions but not all: the voucher was taken more often when the cocaine dose was smaller, and slightly more often when it was for cash than when it was for goods, a difference that cannot be separated from the order of the sessions; with no session offering cocaine without an alternative, the study cannot show how much the vouchers lowered cocaine taking. The four women and two men (aged 30 to 39, recruited in New York City by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements, spending $100 to $500 a week on cocaine; whether they wanted treatment is not stated) each completed eight sessions; in each, after a sample trial, they chose five times, 14 minutes apart, between one dose of smoked cocaine (study conditions: 0, a dummy dose, or 12, 25 or 50 mg, one dose level per session) and a $5 voucher, each choice requiring 200 key presses, and the four money-voucher sessions always came before the four merchandise-voucher sessions. Cocaine choices rose with dose (F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001) and were fewer with the money voucher (F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05), with no significant difference at any single dose. On the editors' reading of the figures, cocaine was chosen on average 10.7 of 20 times with the money voucher and 12.8 with the merchandise voucher (difference 2.2 choices, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation), more than a third of the difference coming from the dummy-dose sessions; with active doses, cocaine was chosen on 60 and 68 of 90 occasions (about 2 in 3 and 3 in 4), at 12 mg about half the time (2.5 and 2.7 of 5) and at 50 mg about 4 times in 5 (3.8 and 4.5 of 5) (Hart et al., 2000). The study measured choices in a laboratory, with small, immediate rewards, not cocaine use outside it; all participants reported using much more cocaine outside the laboratory than in the sessions; the authors' extension to treatment that rewards drug-free tests with vouchers (contingency management) was not tested here; and the earlier laboratory studies they cite, in which larger money alternatives lowered cocaine choice, were not read. Rat studies of choices between cocaine and other rewards are in the answer on the Rat Park studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do people choose other rewards over cocaine when they can? Sometimes. In a lab study, six people who smoked cocaine almost daily chose, many times, between a dose of cocaine and a $5 voucher. With real doses they took the voucher about 1 time in 3 or 4: about half the time at the smallest dose, and less often at the largest. They took a cash voucher a little more often than a voucher for goods, but the cash sessions always came first, so the order may explain it. The study was tiny, measured choices in a lab rather than use in daily life, and never offered cocaine without another choice.

statement: In laboratory experiments that told people they were drinking alcohol or not, and separately gave them alcohol or not, believing they had drunk alcohol increased how much men drank in a short taste test and went with greater sexual arousal, while the alcohol actually drunk, at the low doses these designs allow, affected memory, physical sensations, mood and coordination but not detectably how much people drank; these experiments say little about higher doses or drinking outside the laboratory. In one such experiment in Madison, Wisconsin (published 1973), 64 men, 32 with a history of alcohol problems who were still drinking (treatment admissions, repeated drunkenness arrests, or past membership of Alcoholics Anonymous or a rehabilitation programme; the study's 'alcoholic' group) and 32 social drinkers, were randomly assigned within each group to be told that their drinks were vodka and tonic or tonic only, and to be given one or the other; men told vodka drank about twice as much in a 15-minute taste test as men told tonic (about 18.8 against 9.1 fluid ounces, from the table; the text prints 17.77 for the first; d about 1.1, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.6, editors' calculation), whatever was in the glass and in both groups, while receiving vodka made no detectable difference (13.2 against 14.7 ounces when given tonic; difference −1.5 ounces, 95% CI −5.8 to +2.8, editors' calculation, so a moderate effect cannot be ruled out). Drinking was mostly highest in the first 3 minutes and then fell, with no sign of drinking getting out of control; blood alcohol at the end, estimated rather than measured, averaged 0.031% to 0.093%; there were 8 men per condition; and the men with alcohol problems were older (mean age 46.75 against 37.19 years) (Marlatt et al., 1973). A 1986 meta-analysis of 36 such experiments published before September 1985 found significant pooled effects of believing one had drunk alcohol on sexual arousal (mean g 0.31, 9 studies) and on drinking or wanting to drink (0.52, 3 studies, all in the same direction, this experiment included), none on memory-related information processing, mood, physical sensations, motor performance or bodily arousal, and a non-significant effect in the opposite direction on aggression (−0.13); the alcohol itself impaired information processing (0.53, 5 studies) and motor performance (0.64, 3 studies), changed physical sensations (0.64) and improved mood (0.21), and did not detectably change drinking (−0.04) or sexual arousal (−0.02). The sizes from that analysis are rough: about 35% to 45% of effects of unknown size were set to zero, studies were not weighted, no confidence intervals were given, and doses and participants were not extracted; and in 18 of 20 experiments that did not first ask participants which drink they had received, the alcohol itself changed what they believed they had drunk, so the design seldom separates alcohol from belief (Hull & Bond, 1986). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act? In lab studies, partly yes. In one experiment, 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass; real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more sexual arousal and more drinking, while the alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. These were short lab tests with low doses, mostly from the 1970s and 1980s.
population: Adults in balanced-placebo laboratory experiments published 1973–1985: 64 men with and without a history of alcohol problems in one taste-test experiment in Madison, Wisconsin (Marlatt et al., 1973); participants of 36 experiments whose characteristics and doses the meta-analysis did not extract (Hull & Bond, 1986)
exposure: Being told the drink contained alcohol (against being told it did not), crossed with actually receiving alcohol (against a drink without alcohol), at low doses (study conditions)
comparator: Participants told they were not drinking alcohol; participants given a drink without alcohol
outcome: Amount drunk in a 15-minute taste test; in the meta-analysis, sexual arousal, drinking or desire to drink, aggression, mood, memory-related information processing, motor performance, physical sensations and bodily arousal
magnitude: Marlatt et al. (1973), fluid ounces drunk in 15 minutes: told vodka about 18.8 (Table 1; 17.77 in the text) vs told tonic 9.12, F = 20.59, df 1/56, p < .01, d about 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64; editors' calculation); given vodka 13.19 vs given tonic 14.69, F = .50, difference −1.5 oz (95% CI −5.8 to +2.8; editors' calculation); cell means, men with alcohol problems told tonic 10.94 and 10.25, told vodka 23.87 and 22.13; social drinkers 9.31 and 5.94, 14.62 and 14.44; estimated end-of-task blood alcohol .031% to .093%. risk_of_bias.note: The 1973 experiment assigned men at random within each group, but sequence generation and concealment are not reported, the experimenter who mixed the drinks and gave the instructions knew each assignment, and no standard deviations are printed (card sc_marlatt_1973: RoB 2 some concerns); the meta-analysis has critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (undescribed search, effects of unknown size set to zero, unweighted means without intervals, primary studies' randomization not appraised, experimenters blind in only 7 of 36 studies; card sc_hull_1986).

inconsistency.note: The three drinking studies point the same way (0.66, 0.52, 0.39; heterogeneity chi-square(2) = 0.32); expectancy effects on other behaviours differ by type, which the statement reports type by type.

indirectness.note: Low doses (blood alcohol estimated at 0.03% to 0.09% in the drinking experiment), a 15-minute taste test and laboratory measures, in samples from the 1970s and early 1980s, mostly men where described; the meta-analysis's drinking category mixes amounts drunk with counts of sips.

imprecision.note: The effect of belief on the amount drunk is precise enough for its direction (d 1.13, 0.63 to 1.64, editors' calculation); the absence of an effect of alcohol on drinking is imprecise and is stated as such; the meta-analysis gives no intervals, so its sizes are called rough.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the meta-analysis (published studies only); with three drinking studies, small-study effects cannot be judged.

grade.reasoning: Randomized factorial experiments start high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. 'Increases' rests on random assignment of the instructions within the experiments and applies to the laboratory conditions stated; whether belief changes drinking at higher doses or outside a laboratory is not claimed. The comparison of men with and without alcohol problems is not randomized (they differed in age and social class) and is not used for any causal statement. Status replicated: the three balanced-placebo studies of drinking or desire to drink, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986), point the same way; the 1973 experiment is one of them and the other two were not read. The meta-analysis's conclusions that alcohol and expectancy rarely interact (7 of 137 tests significant) and that the design is no longer needed are not used: a count of significant tests cannot show that interactions are absent (card interpretation gap). Doses appear only as study conditions.

statement: In studies published from 2000 to 2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and eight other European countries, mostly surveys in which health professionals reported their own attitudes, many professionals described negative attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug problems, or regarded them less well than patients with other conditions, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services, while several studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes; whether such attitudes make the care these patients receive worse was examined in only a few studies, whose results point different ways. A systematic review of 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples; 12 from Australia, 7 from the UK and 5 from the US; 20 quantitative, mostly questionnaires at one time point, five interview or focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two using observation) gave no count or pooled estimate of how common negative attitudes were. Among its examples: among 866 professionals in eight European countries, regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with patients with depression or diabetes, and lowest among doctors outside specialist drug and alcohol services; in a vignette study, professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness; and at least six study summaries in the review's table describe attitudes as moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive (editors' count). More contact, experience, training and support went with more positive attitudes, in data collected at one time. On consequences for care: clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney who perceived more discrimination by staff were less likely to complete treatment (a mixed-methods study of 92 clients, attributed in the review's text to the wrong paper by the same team); two qualitative studies suggested that clinicians may impose their beliefs on patients, and described district nurses making shorter, task-focused visits; among 2,864 patients with HIV, 17.1% of them currently injecting drugs, physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reports of problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or access; and the one included study that observed care, 683 visits to nine psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986, found better care for patients with substance use problems than for other patients on all four criteria, a result the review's text does not mention (van Boekel et al., 2013). The review searched three databases in English and Dutch, excluded studies from Asia, Africa and South America and studies of training, weighted all studies equally whatever their response rate (31% to 92% where given), and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 by the study card; its abstract's statements that negative attitudes reduced patients' empowerment and treatment outcomes rest on two qualitative studies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently? In studies from 2000 to 2011, mostly surveys, many health workers said they felt negatively about patients with drug or alcohol problems, or less positive than about patients with other illnesses, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services; some studies found neutral or positive views. Whether this changes care was studied only a few times, and the results differed: in one study, people who felt treated unfairly by staff were less likely to finish treatment; in another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care; and the one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
population: Health professionals (nurses, doctors, staff of drug, alcohol and mental-health services, mixed groups) and, in five papers, their patients, in 28 papers published 2000–2011 from Australia, the UK, the USA, Canada, Ireland and eight European countries
exposure: Being a patient with an alcohol or drug use disorder (the patient group professionals were asked about or treated)
comparator: Patients with other conditions (for example depression, diabetes or other mental illness) where studies compared them; otherwise none
outcome: Professionals' self-reported attitudes, regard and implicit associations; patients' perceived discrimination, treatment completion and reports of care; observed quality of care
magnitude: No pooled estimate and no count of studies by direction. As reported by van Boekel et al. (2013): 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples); regard lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems among 866 professionals in 8 European countries; at least 6 of the study summaries describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes (editors' count of Table 5); 5 papers link more experience or contact with more positive attitudes. Consequences: perceived staff discrimination predicted not completing treatment (92 clients, Sydney); physicians' attitudes not associated with patients' reports of care (2,864 patients with HIV, 373 physicians; 23.2% of the patients had physicians with negative attitudes towards people who inject drugs); better care for patients with substance use problems on all 4 criteria in 683 observed emergency visits (California, 1985–1986).

risk_of_bias.note: A systematic review with critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (no protocol; three databases in English and Dutch, PsycINFO giving 10 records; no list of excluded studies; studies weighted equally whatever their design or response rate, from 31% to 92%; conclusions about consequences not tempered by the designs behind them; card sc_van_boekel_2013), whose primary studies are mostly self-reported attitudes from self-selected respondents.

inconsistency.note: Attitude findings and consequence findings both point in different directions; the statement reports both directions and the status is mixed, so the claim is not downgraded twice for the same problem.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes what professionals reported, in the countries and years covered, and says that care itself was rarely measured.

imprecision.note: Not applicable to a narrative description without pooled estimates.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not judged for a descriptive summary.

grade.reasoning: Observational studies (mostly cross-sectional surveys and qualitative studies) seen through one systematic review: starts low; down one for risk of bias: very low. Rated as worded: the statement describes what the included studies reported, not how common negative attitudes are (the review gives no count), and gives the evidence on care as a handful of studies pointing different ways, including the observational study finding better care that the review leaves out of its text and the null survey result it notes without weighing (card reporting issues). Not used: the abstract's statements that negative attitudes diminished empowerment and treatment outcomes (two qualitative studies), and the recommendation of training (cross-sectional associations, after studies of training were excluded). A causal claim, that health workers' attitudes worsen care, would be insufficient evidence. Status mixed: findings on attitudes and on consequences differ between studies without an explanation the review can settle. statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release, and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate was 1,612 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release, against 725 (625 to 831) over the whole follow-up and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release; the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because in some cohorts deaths in custody had been recorded as deaths on the day of release, which inflated the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years, falling to 826 in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers whose certification and coding were not checked across countries and decades; and it recorded nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance, so it cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Is the time just after leaving prison more dangerous? Yes, most of all the first week. In about 1.5 million people released from prison in eight countries, deaths in days 2 to 7 after release were about 1.5 to 2 times as common as in the weeks that followed. Poisoning by alcohol or other drugs was the most common cause of death, in that first week and overall. Still, 91 in 100 of these poisoning deaths happened more than 4 weeks after release. The records did not say which drugs were involved, and nobody measured drug use or tolerance, so the study cannot say why the first week is riskier.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the all-cause first-week pattern: complete release cohorts linked to death registers and analysed under one plan, with sensitivity analyses for deaths in custody recorded on the day of release and for time back in custody (720 against 725). The cause-specific figures are less certain: death certification, toxicology and the coding of drug deaths and of undetermined intent were not appraised across eight countries and four decades (card sc_borschmann_2024: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and three Western Australian cohorts overlap in place and time.

inconsistency.note: I² is 91% for days 2–7 and 99–100% over the whole follow-up, and cohort rates range from 236 to 1,183, but the first-week excess holds in the pooled rate ratios with moderate heterogeneity (I² 26% against week 2); the heterogeneity concerns the size of the rates, which the statement gives with their range.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded for these mostly high-income cohorts, mostly men; the statement says that the poisoning category names no drug and includes alcohol and deaths of undetermined intent.

imprecision.note: The days 2–7 intervals are wide (all causes 1,048 to 2,287; poisoning 332 to 1,076), but the rate ratios against later periods exclude 1 (1.5, 1.2 to 1.8).

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the study; an individual participant data consortium analysed under one plan is less exposed to selective publication.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.
